To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

A2A receptor‐deficient mice generated on the CD1 genetic background show an increased sensitivity to ethanol‐induced anxiolytic‐locomotor effects, but they are less sensitive to the rewarding properties of the drug.
A2A receptors play a role in ethanol consumption and in the motivational and anxiolytic properties of ethanol.
A2A receptor knockout mice, generated on a CD-1 background, are characterized by high ethanol consumption, which is accompanied by an enhanced locomotor stimulant and anxiolytic effect of ethanol.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of the A2A receptor as a potential therapeutic target in ethanol abuse and dependence.
the development of a novel therapeutic approach to the treatment of alcoholism based on the modulation of the A2AR.
the development of new therapeutic targets for the treatment of alcoholism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

A2AR deficiency is associated with a high ethanol consumption that seems to be related with a decreased aversive motivational properties of ethanol, an increased locomotor‐stimulating and anxiolytic properties of ethanol and an increased sensitivity of ethanol to induce locomotor sensitization.

A2AR knockout mice produced on CD1 genetic background show a high propensity to consume and prefer ethanol that is associated with altered sensitivity in the anxiolytics, locomotor effects and CPP of ethanol, but not with alteration in the motivational effects of ethanol as tested in the CTA paradigm.
A2AR knockout mice generated on CD1 background display a phenotype characterized by high ethanol consumption and a high sensitivity to the anabolic and anxiolytic effect of ethanol.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

A2ARs are not involved in the motivational effects of ethanol, and that A2AR deficiency is a risk factor for ethanol consumption, which could be associated with increased sensitivity to the stimulant and anxiolytic properties of ethanol.
the adenosinergic system is an important regulator of alcohol consumption and preference.
the A2A receptor may play a role in the motivational effects of ethanol, although the genetic background of the mice may be critical in determining the behavioral effects of A2AR deficiency.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the A2AR may be a potential therapeutic target to reduce ethanol consumption and preference.
the A2AR plays a role in the motivational and locomotor effects of alcohol and that these effects are influenced by the genetic background.
A2AR antagonism may be useful to reduce ethanol consumption and preference.
